When that Truth is personally experienced and made real, the Sufi becomes a free human being. The mystic’s calling does not stand opposed to prophetic revelation. It fulfills revelation, because it brings to life revelation's hidden truth. Without this inner truth, nothing remains but an abstract monotheism (tawhîd), an assertion of God's oneness that has not become a lived experience. Only the idea—or, better, the actual experience—of theophany, the manifestation of God, can overcome it.

The divine essence is unknowable, yet God's actions are manifestations through which the divine attributes appear. Such a manifestation is not God taking bodily form. To perceive a theophany is to perceive the double meaning (iltibâs) of every manifest being: how it conceals and reveals the invisible at one and the same time. Without the awareness that makes this vision possible, we remain in a world of duality and opposing things. In that condition, both the devout believer and the dogmatic theologian are, at heart, polytheists without knowing it.

Such awareness cannot awaken by turning away from what is visible and perceptible to the senses. The visible must first be recognized as a veil, and then transformed into a mirror. Among all human experiences, one holds a special place: only the experience of human love for a beautiful person can lead us to live through this transformation—the soul's shock and ecstasy before a divine manifestation. Ruzbihan gives Sufism a decisive new direction by distinguishing two kinds of seekers.

There are pious ascetics for whom human love has played no part at the beginning of the spiritual path. And there are those for whom human love is the beginning of divine love, because the two belong to one and the same book, the book of one and the same love—though its text must be learned and read. Only this second group, of which Ruzbihan is the outstanding example, deserves the name Faithful of Love, a name chosen for their kinship with the Fedeli d’amore, Dante's companions in love.

Along this same path, Ruzbihan does not shrink from appearing as a malâmati: one of those who, in order to conceal the purity of their inner face, sometimes deliberately behave in ways that invite public blame. From this point of view he may be considered a forerunner of another celebrated man of Shiraz, the great poet Hafez, whose dîwân, or collected poems, Iranian Sufis have always known how to read as a reminder of the mystical path.

At a friend's request, Ruzbihan composed a “spiritual journal,” an invaluable document in the mystical literature of any age. It calls to mind certain passages from Swedenborg's Memorabilia. This is a record of Ruzbihan's visions and dreams from the age of fifteen. It shows that even as a child he possessed extraordinary emotional intensity and a remarkable gift for visions.

At fifteen, he left his home. A vision revealed his secret rank in the mystical hierarchy. Then came a succession of magnificent visions: angels and beings of beauty, flowering landscapes, crimson dawns... All Ruzbihan's books are written in a highly individual language, alive with an almost unbroken ecstatic lyricism that does not always make for easy reading.

Yet this autobiographical journal gives us the testimony of lived experience from which to trace the stages and trials through which the unfolding drama of love leads, by way of theophanies, to the inner realization of divine oneness (tawhîd).
The first trial is the trial of the Veil. Here Ruzbihan certainly stands within the great Sufi tradition.

But he adds an extraordinary insight of his own, bringing both experiential mysticism and speculative mystical thought to one of their highest points. The “Hidden Treasure” brought the world into existence so that it might be known, and might know itself through its creatures. Spirit is the primordial foundation through which the Holy Spirits endure—the spiritual identities of beings, existing from before all time. Every atom of existence is, no doubt, an eye wholly absorbed in contemplating the Light from which it came.

But the Divine Being then experiences jealousy toward himself. By making himself an object to himself, by revealing himself, he is no longer simply his own witness: now there is a witness outside himself, someone other than himself. This is the first Veil.

The Divine Being therefore seeks to regain possession of himself. He turns that Spirit away from contemplating him and directs his creature to contemplate itself. This vision of the self by the self is the second Veil. The trial of the Veil is the very meaning of Creation. The descent of the Holy Spirits into earthly existence has no other purpose than to bring them through this trial to victory.

To pass through it, the mystic must discover that his self-knowledge is the very gaze by which God contemplates himself, that he himself is the witness through whom God bears witness to himself. The veil then becomes a mirror.

But to look for something beyond the Veil, Ruzbihan says, is to fall into the “madness of the unattainable.” Since Creation, God has never looked upon a world other than himself: such a world is abhorrent to him. Those who awaken to their calling as witnesses are the eyes through which God still looks at the world, and through which the world still matters to him. They may be unknown to everyone; nonetheless, it is thanks to them that the world endures.

Far beyond any social role, these mystics fulfill a function of cosmic salvation. Here Ruzbihan's insight comes remarkably close to that of Meister Eckhart. The gaze with which I know God is none other than the gaze with which God knows me. That is the secret of the theophanic visions through which Ruzbihan moves toward the inner experience of divine oneness.

It is the unfolding dialectic of love that makes this progress possible, for love alone reveals the identity of witness and witnessed, contemplator and contemplated. That dialectic fills an entire Persian work, perhaps Ruzbihan's masterpiece: The Jasmine of the Faithful of Love. “With the eyes of the heart I contemplated uncreated Beauty; with the eyes of the intellect I strove to understand the secret of the Human Form.” The drama of love unveils the secret of divine manifestations because a theophany is, in its essence, the appearance of the divine in beauty.

Our age of “demythologization” has labored so hard to strip beauty of its sacred character that the feeling of the numinous—the presence of the holy—in the face of beauty may now seem strange, even utterly foreign. For all our Iranian Faithful of Love, by contrast, it is a fundamental experience. The same is true of Ibn Arabi, who influenced the whole of Islamic spirituality for eight centuries and remains one of the most distinguished witnesses to this mystical religion of beauty as the supreme divine attribute.

Ruzbihan embraces the Neoplatonic proposition: “Even before the worlds existed, the Divine Being was himself love, lover, and beloved.” He is immediately faced with the great question that had exercised Sufi circles from the beginning: is it fitting to use the word love in speaking of God? Whom does the mystic love when he speaks of his love for God? The whole of The Jasmine answers these questions in a sequence of chapters.

On one side, it explores the prophetic meaning of beauty, contemplating the Prophet of Islam as the prophet of the religion of beauty. On the other, drawing on all the resources of Platonic inspiration, it unveils the eternal source of love, bringing together the great themes of the Eternal Witness and the Eternal Bride. Suhrawardi had already set us on this path toward the transfiguration of Eros.

Here, too, love is not transferred from one object to another, from a human object to a divine one. What takes place instead is a transformation of the person who loves. That transformation finds its emblem in Majnun and Layla—the Tristan and Isolde of the mystical epic, in Persian as in Arabic. At the height of his love, Majnun becomes the “mirror of God.” It is God himself who, in the lover's gaze upon the beloved, contemplates his own eternal face.

This is what it means to attain the vision of vision, the inner realization of oneness through identity, in which there is no longer either I + I or I = I, but I × I = I. Then, in the intoxication of a consciousness that has passed beyond itself, the mystic may utter the celebrated, extravagant cry of al-Hallaj: Anâ’l-Haqq (“I am God”). The case of al-Hallaj occupied Ruzbihan throughout his life. He offered abundant explanations and defenses of that famous “theopathic utterance,” a saying in which the divine speaks through the mystic.

Indeed, it is to Ruzbihan that we owe the preservation of a work by al-Hallaj in his own substantial Commentary on the Paradoxes of the Sufis. We published the Persian text some years ago; it is a veritable compendium of the Sufism of Ruzbihan's time.

Book IV returns to a question first raised in Book I: the relationship between Shiism and Sufism. Its four chapters examine the writings of four important authors from the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries CE. Unfortunately, the second of these authors remains anonymous.

I. The first chapter is devoted to Sayyed Haydar Amoli (born 720 AH/1320 CE; died after 787 AH/1385–86 CE). His extensive writings, frequently cited by later authors, had until now remained unpublished. We have recently prepared editions of two of his treatises, together forming a true compendium of Shia philosophy. For many of his other works, unfortunately, we have still been unable to locate manuscripts.

Haydar Amoli came from northern Iran. He spent the first half of his life in his native Tabaristan, a province now part of Mazandaran on the southern shore of the Caspian Sea. The works we have so far been able to study supply the materials for a moving spiritual autobiography, particularly characteristic of an Iranian spiritual seeker. Born into a distinguished Shia family of Tabaristan, Sayyed Haydar studied, among other places, in Isfahan.

Until the age of thirty, he enjoyed a brilliant, privileged youth. He even served as his ruler's minister and was briefly caught up in the upheavals of his time. Then a profound spiritual crisis caused him to renounce every worldly ambition and set out upon the roads as a “pilgrim of God,” wearing the poor cloak of a Sufi. He traveled to the Shia holy places of Iraq, where he spent the entire second period of his life producing a body of work on an immense scale.

These writings mark a major moment in the development of Shia philosophy and spirituality. They alone are enough to show that Shia thought, as such, is not—as some modernists would have it—a political invention of the Safavid period. They are also among the works that offer an answer to the difficult question of the original relationship between Shiism and Sufism.

On a matter so decisive for our understanding of Islamic spirituality generally, the student of religion prefers to let those directly concerned speak for themselves and to be guided by their answers. This is why the texts of Haydar Amoli have already played such an important part in Book I.

Haydar confronts the question directly, apparently because it arose with particular urgency for him and those around him. His answer is that of a seeker of inner meaning, for whom Shiism is, in essence, the inward or esoteric dimension of Islam. Any Shia Muslim who confines himself to outward religious forms therefore mutilates the very teaching of the holy Imams. The Sufis, by contrast, affirm the inner meaning of divine revelations and thus show themselves to be the “true Shia.” Unfortunately, they have forgotten their origins and have mutilated their own inner teaching insofar as they have excluded the doctrine of the Imams.

Sayyed Haydar wants to put an end to this situation once and for all. He takes issue equally with Shia who denounce Sufism and Sufis who denounce Shiism. He must therefore contend on several fronts: with the legalistic outlook of Sunni Islam, with Shia who have forgotten the inner meaning of their faith, and with Sufis who have forgotten both their origins and what they fundamentally owe to Shiism. Two centuries later Mulla Sadra Shirazi would face a similar situation. It is, indeed, a tragic situation that spiritual seekers in each of the three branches of the Abrahamic tradition have had to confront in their own ways.

In meeting these challenges, Sayyed Haydar acts as a disciple of Ibn Arabi, to whom he refers repeatedly. Much of his effort goes into tracing the passage from the theological tawhîd—the affirmation of divine oneness to which the prophets called humanity—to the ontological tawhîd, the realization of oneness at the level of being, to which the “Friends of God” invite us in the wake of the holy Imams.

These pages show how fully Shia Iranian thought was able to make Ibn Arabi's spiritual philosophy its own, precisely because it found there something that already belonged to it. Ibn Arabi's Fosûs (The Bezels of Wisdom) could themselves be seen as belonging to the phenomenon of the Holy Book, since their author had received their heavenly inspiration from the Prophet.

Yet, despite his devotion to Ibn Arabi's thought and writings, Haydar Amoli disagrees with him on one point that admits no compromise: the very point that, for a Shia Muslim, determines the meaning of prophecy.

Like all Twelver Shia, Haydar holds that the Seal of walâyat—the inner spiritual reality of prophecy—cannot be a prophet, namely Jesus, as Ibn Arabi maintained. That Seal is, and can only be, the Muhammadan Imamate: in the person of the First Imam as the Seal of universal walâyat, and in the person of the Twelfth Imam as the Seal of Muhammadan walâyat. The entire destiny of Shia sacred history is at stake here—a vision of history whose full significance Book VII will reveal—and Haydar Amoli cannot yield.

Like so many of his fellow mystics, Sayyed Haydar possessed an unusual gift for visions in the mundus imaginalis, the imaginal world. This went hand in hand with his fondness for diagrams. His diagram of a vision beheld in the night sky over Baghdad provides a striking illustration of the structure of the heavenly assembly of the “Fourteen Immaculate Ones.”

II. The second chapter studies a treatise from the same period whose author, unfortunately, remains unknown. It offers an extensive commentary on a famous hadith, or saying attributed to the Prophet: “The Qur’an has an outer meaning and an inner meaning; that inner meaning in turn has an inner meaning, and so on through seven depths of hidden meaning.”

In setting out this golden rule of spiritual interpretation—the progressive inward discovery of the meaning of Qur’anic revelation—the hadith returns us to the “phenomenon of the Holy Book,” examined at length in Book I as the very foundation upon which the meaning and calling of Shiism depend. In this respect, the anonymous treatise stands between the great work of scriptural interpretation by Semnani, examined below, and that of Haydar Amoli, who devoted a monumental work in six large volumes to the Shia spiritual interpretation of the Qur’an.

The anonymous author frames the problem in terms familiar to every interpreter of the Abrahamic tradition: what is the relation between a revealed text expressed in a particular language at a particular moment and the eternal truth it proclaims? How are we to understand the passage from the divine Word to its expression in human speech?

The obvious objection is this: if the divine Word is eternal, and if the events it reveals must therefore also be eternal, what becomes of the very idea of an event? The author answers by proposing precisely the idea of an eternal event. For such an event, “before” and “after” cannot be understood in terms of the measurable, irreversible time of chronological history.

If the phenomenon of the Book marks the entry of the divine Word into time, spiritual interpretation (ta’wîl) leads that Word back to a time that is not the time of history. Here we see the interpretation of the Book at work: it was this that led our thinkers to confront and master the problem of historical time.

As for the seven depths of inner meaning, each is identified by a name for the Book drawn from the Qur’an itself. Each name corresponds to a level of meaning and, consequently, to the group of people capable of understanding at that level. The interpretation of scripture is thus inseparable from a philosophical understanding of the human being.
We shall see this fundamental connection confirmed twice more below. It is characteristic of a spirituality founded upon the many levels at which the Holy Book can mean something and be understood.

III. The third chapter examines a work of spiritual interpretation by Sa'in al-Din Isfahani (d. 830 AH/1427 CE), a thinker who belonged to an entire family line of Shia philosophers and spiritual teachers. The work interprets a particularly enigmatic Qur’anic verse: “The Hour drew near, and the Moon was split” (54:1). The author offers, as it were, a practical exercise in interpretation, beautifully illustrating the connection already discussed between our understanding of the human being and our understanding of scripture: between ways of being and ways of understanding, between levels of understanding and the people who inhabit them.

By interpreting this verse on several levels of meaning, he is able to sketch a religious typology embracing all the forms of religious consciousness then found within Islam. In order of increasing penetration into inner meaning, these are: jurists and transmitters of tradition (specialists in hadith); Islamic theologians (here, the scholastic thinkers of kalâm); the Peripatetic philosophers; the Ishrâqîyûn, or Platonists who followed Suhrawardi; Sufis; Hurufis; and Shia.

Once again, through the author's own words, we encounter the serious question: can there truly be a doctrine of prophecy, or an authentic Sufism, without the Shia understanding of the Imams? These philosophical ideas are expressed in a way that makes it appropriate to speak of a doctrine of the Imams that does not dare—or no longer dares—to speak its own name. This is one of the tragic aspects of the history of Shia thought.

IV. The fourth and final chapter of this book is devoted to the writings and teachings of one of the greatest masters of Iranian spirituality, Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 736 AH/1336 CE). By a paradox that is sadly far from unique, his works, in Persian and Arabic, still exist entirely in manuscript. He belonged to the generation before Haydar Amoli.

Like Haydar, he experienced a profound spiritual crisis: once a young page at the court of the Mongol ruler Arghun, he became a Sufi. His teaching stands in the line of Najm al-Din Kubra (d. 1221), the great master of Central Asian Sufism who was the first to pay close attention to the colored lights whose aura appears to the spiritual awareness of mystics.

Semnani's teaching is marked by an interpretation of scripture that pushes the inward understanding of Qur’anic revelation to its furthest limit. The relationship discussed above—between scriptural interpretation and the understanding of the human being, between levels of meaning and levels of comprehension—takes on an entirely original form here, joining a theory of colored lights perceived in the mundus imaginalis. At the same time, the succession of the prophets is itself understood in a radically inward way. That succession revives, within Islam, the teaching of the Verus Propheta, the “True Prophet,” found in early Judeo-Christianity.

The inward transformation takes place through a physiology of the subtle organism concealed beneath the human physical body. This subtle physiology has seven centers or organs, called latîfa. They are not, as in Schiller, the “stars of your destiny,” but the “prophets of your being.” Each embodies a prophet, from the “Adam of your being,” through the “Abraham of your being,” to the “Muhammad of your being.” Each latîfa has its own aura, its own colored light. The mystic's perception of that light reveals how far the subtle body has developed—in other words, the body of resurrection.

Every passage of the Qur’an concerning one of the prophets must then be understood as referring to the corresponding subtle organ or center. In Sa'in al-Din Isfahani's typology, levels of understanding were distributed among different groups of people. Here they are brought entirely within the individual: each level corresponds to one of the subtle centers or organs of the spiritual seeker.

Above the seven latîfa of the “prophets of your being” there is another, to which Semnani makes several mysterious allusions. He names it after the very angel of knowledge and revelation: the latîfa jabra’êliya, the “angel Gabriel of your being.” It is at this summit of mystical understanding of the human being that we glimpse, in Semnani, the secret of a doctrine of the Imams that once again does not dare, or does not wish, to speak its name.

Semnani analyzes and describes in detail the cosmic agents and influences that constitute the seven latîfa. His is a magnificent vision, steeped in tradition yet deeply personal. Semnani the mystic reveals himself as a profound metaphysician, whose system invites comparison on many fronts. His work therefore marks a decisive moment not only in Iran's spiritual culture, but in the wider study of metaphysics and mysticism.

I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

The Quranic sura of the Dawn offers this invitation: “O soul at peace, return to your Lord, content with Him and pleasing to Him” (89:27–28). Comparing the interpretations given to this verse within Islam brings into focus the different spiritual attitudes that Muslims and Christians have associated with peace of soul. And within Islam itself, the interpretations offered by mystics and spiritual writers reveal another contrast: that between the inward religion of Sufism, with its mystical knowledge, and a religion understood primarily in terms of law, whenever the latter refuses to make room for the esoteric dimension of faith—that is, for the inner life of those whose very souls are turned inward.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

The subject of this book is Ruzbihan Baqli of Shiraz (522/1128–606/1209), one of the most representative figures of Iranian Sufism, though not himself a Shiite Sufi. We have referred to him in the preceding pages, and have already had occasion, as we shall again, to raise the unavoidable question of the relationship between Shiism and Sufism. Haydar Amoli will have much to tell us about this (see below, Book IV, Chapter I).
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

For now, let us recall two fundamental ideas in Shiite teachings about prophecy and the Imams (see above, Book I): the prophetic mission (nobowwat) and walayat. The latter term, as we have seen, describes the special standing of the Twelve Imams as those whom God loves, the “Friends of God,” and the protective, guiding role they exercise toward their followers. From the followers, in turn, comes a corresponding love for the Imams. At its heart, therefore, the religion of the Imams reveals itself as a religion of love.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

We have already observed that, from the standpoint of divine wisdom, one could very briefly express the difference between Shiism and Sunnism in this way: everything that Shiite spiritual knowledge sees centered on the Imam as its pole is, in Sunnism, invested in the Prophet alone. The resulting imbalance is one we have already begun to discern.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

One symptom appears in the fate of that central Shiite idea, walayat. Sufism outside Shiism generally speaks instead of wilayat: a state of intimacy with God attained through renunciation of the self. In the West, the customary translation has become “sainthood.”
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

But to ask about the relative standing of nobowwat and wilayat—whether a prophet is superior to a “saint,” or a “saint” to a prophet—without taking account of the specifically Shiite understanding of the relationship between nobowwat and walayat is to distort the entire teaching about prophecy.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

The real question is this: how can wilayat exist without walayat, or how is it connected to it? Some connection there must be, since at the root of the spiritual lineage of almost every Sufi tariqa, or initiatory path, we eventually find one of the Imams. The result is a situation we shall later describe as “a teaching about the Imams that no longer dares speak its own name” (see below, Book IV, Chapter III).
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

An ambiguity remains, one that weighs upon tawhid, the affirmation of divine unity, and must continually be overcome. How does the divine Being, beyond words and beyond anything that can be said of it, reveal itself to a human being? Elsewhere, in studying the teachings of Qazi Sa'id Qommi, we have shown how Shiite spiritual philosophy, drawing on the words of the Imams themselves, understands the Face that God turns toward humanity as, by that very fact, the Face humanity turns toward God. That Face is the Imam.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

Without it—as though Christianity were deprived of Christ—the mystic is exposed to the paradox and intoxication that burst forth in the cry Ana'l-Haqq, “I am God.” More fundamentally still, the very practice of Sufism presupposes an answer to this question: can love have a place in the relationship between God and humanity, and between humanity and God? In the religion of the Imams, the Imam as a figure of divine self-revelation provides the mediation that makes the answer possible. As we shall see, this is precisely the central problem Ruzbihan's spiritual life had to confront, together with the related problem of how divine love and human love are connected.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

Here we are only pointing to the problem. Other questions will arise later, or will have to be treated elsewhere. There is, for instance, the severity with which Imam Reza spoke of certain Sufis. There is the fact that many Iranian Shiite spiritual teachers use the language of Sufism without being Sufis in any formal sense; strictly speaking, therefore, tasawwuf, or Sufism, does not encompass everything meant by Islamic mysticism.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

There is the possibility that the dominant place given to the shaykh, or spiritual master, may amount to an appropriation of the Imam's role. And there is a monistic metaphysics, professed in extreme forms by certain Sufis, which many Shiite spiritual thinkers reject.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

We shall leave these issues aside and consider Ruzbihan alone, struggling with his own experiences and his own questions. His case is especially fascinating. Rather than burden it with comparisons or with a history of Sufism from its beginnings, we want simply to allow Ruzbihan's own distinctive voice to reach us: the particular intensity of his mystical feeling, the character of his visions, however formidable the difficulties of his language and style.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

In short, we want him to show us, through his own words, why we call his Sufism the way of the “Faithful of Love.” Some pages of his writings may express something unique in the whole literature of mysticism.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

Yet whatever the differences between Shiite and non-Shiite Sufism, there is a shared spiritual attitude underlying everything that belongs to Sufism. That same attitude characterizes the inner, esoteric dimension proper to Islam as a prophetic religion. It helps us recognize both the affinities and the differences between this tradition and what is called “Christian esotericism.” In the Christian world, the Church developed in such a way that every esoteric current took shape on the margins of the official Churches, forming an “inner Church.” Sufism does not stand on the margins: it is the spiritual tradition of Islam.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

By Sufism we mean the word in its broadest sense, not merely those outward forms and secondary practices that “modernists” use as an excuse to condemn and reject it, sometimes furiously. It is a tradition that does not even need archives: as we have noted, some Sufi paths have left, or will leave, no visible material trace. Such traces are beside the point. What matters is a spiritual attitude opposed to the will to power—an attitude in which any disturbance of the soul's peace may appear as the supreme paradox.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

The phenomenon Hegel taught us to call the “unhappy consciousness” belongs, in a distinctive way, to the inner life of Christianity. It is true that certain forms of Christian consciousness today claim to be increasingly “present in this world,” in the hope of becoming less and less “unhappy.”
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

But that changes nothing about the place, within Sufism, of a contradiction to be overcome, an absence to be filled, a spiritual struggle to be sustained. What differs profoundly is the nature of the opposing terms, at least if we look for their Christian expression in the teachings of official dogmatic theology. We are familiar with such oppositions as sin and justifying grace, or faith and knowledge—believing and knowing.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

We are equally familiar with another opposition said to follow from them, commonly and crudely framed as “mysticism” versus “sensuality”: as though love of God excluded love for a created being, as though beauty were a demonic trap, as though traditional asceticism had no response to doubts about these claims except to denounce a revival of “paganism.” Our secular sociologies have simply recorded these oppositions; one could hardly expect them to do more. In a society we might briefly call “post-Christian,” people may no longer speak of sin, but they speak of a “guilt complex.”
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

Is the symptom not the same? Does it not betray the same sickness of the “unhappy consciousness”? As for the supposedly “broad-minded” concessions, the servile accommodations to what is called the “modern spirit,” we need only look at some examples of what, in a bitter reversal of meaning, is still called “sacred art.” It becomes clear that their inspiration is far removed from the Renaissance longing for a beauty banished from the world by the consciousness of sin.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

Alongside these conflicts inherited from our moral tradition are others of a more specifically intellectual kind: the opposition between historical fact and inner truth, between what historical faith takes as its object and a spiritual reality not dependent on an event in historical time; the opposition between the literal form of what revelation gives us and its spiritual meaning, between dogmatic consciousness and a consciousness that perceives all outward things as symbols.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

These oppositions run so deep that they persist even where we might expect secularization to have made them disappear. They may depend, above all, on what we call historical consciousness: on the assumption that the material historicity of irreversible events is the measure of value and the guarantee of truth. The burden of historical consciousness, which has weighed tragically on so many Christian souls since Origen, has never been heavier than in the sociological philosophies of the “post-Christian” world.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

Yet the Quranic words “O soul at peace, return, content and pleasing...” speak to the Sufi from within a spiritual universe foreign to these assumptions and oppositions. There is something astonishing, even tragic, in the fact that contemporary philosophical exchanges between East and West so rarely reach the heart of the matter. A Sufism conscious of its own meaning, and of what it undoubtedly shares with a very ancient Christianity, would have its own refusals and affirmations to set against a conformism so adept at disguising itself that it manages to pass for a force of liberation.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

The Sufi does not think of himself as a sinner; he feels no need to be “justified.” He is an exile. And his distress, his longing—a longing he shares with the spiritual seekers of every age—makes him yearn, from the depths of his being, for a messenger, a teacher of truth, a spiritual Guide who can show him the road home.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

No other future is desirable or even imaginable to him than to find again the place from which he came, to be at home once more. The post-Christian person may no longer be a “sinner,” but is even less willing to be an “exile”: he wants to make his home in this world.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

Yet he may be driven out of it at any hour of day or night, without ever having suspected the path onto which he will then be cast. The idea of the Guide is inseparable from that of the prophet (see the discussion of prophecy above, Book I). A prophet's function is not exhausted by the giving of laws.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

Rather, the purpose of the shari'a, the revealed law, is to open the Path (tariqa) toward rediscovered spiritual Truth (haqiqa). So, although a contrast has elsewhere been drawn between prophetic religion and mystical religion, for the Sufi mystical religion is the truth—the true meaning of prophetic revelation—just as the prophet's task is to open to the seeker of spiritual knowledge the path of Return (ma'ad).
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

We can already begin to see that a certain opposition, increasingly prominent in Christianity, presents itself quite differently to the Sufi. On one side stands what is called the natural meaning of scriptural Revelation, identified with historical truth; on the other, its spiritual or esoteric meaning. Matters have been made worse because this spiritual meaning has so often been confused with allegory, or tolerated by the Church's teaching authority only when confined to a typology that remains entirely within the bounds of empirical history.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

For the Sufi, this is neither a choice between two meanings nor the addition of some higher structure to the literal one. It is a passage to be made, a passage on which spiritual birth depends. Every genuine interpretation of scripture—that is, every spiritual interpretation—is an exodus of the soul.

Because the Sufi is not captive to the assumptions of our historical consciousness, the opposition we have established between contingent factual truth and eternal truth becomes, for him, an inward pilgrimage: from the shari'a to the haqiqa. Literal revelation (tanzil) is transfigured through the interpretation that brings out its hidden meaning (ta'wil). That meaning refers to real events, but events taking place on a plane other than the one we call History.

Islamic society has not developed anything comparable to what we call the Church. A Sufi would find it utterly incomprehensible to be told that he must receive his faith, and therefore eternal life, from “the Church.” Even if theology, having become atheistic, gives way to sociology, the Sufi remains a witness standing in accusation. He has his own resources for resisting the demands that collective consciousness imposes.

In their place he sets the personal bond between disciple and initiator, the bond with the Guide, the shaykh or pir; or, in Shiism, the bond with the Imam, above all the Hidden Imam. In Sufism this corresponds to the bond with a personal heavenly Guide, whom Najm al-Din Kubra calls the invisible master (shaykh al-ghayb), the Witness in Heaven (shahid fi'l-sama'). It would be hard to find a more radical basis for safeguarding spiritual individuality, once and for all. This individuality, of course, is not the everyday ego represented by the nafs ammara, the commanding soul with its disorderly appetites.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

It is what our authors call the “Holy Spirit” within a human being: the higher self, existing before earthly life, which must be freed or won back. That is precisely the aim of the whole spiritual struggle of Sufism: to subdue the nafs ammara and transform it into the nafs motma'yanna, the “soul at peace.” This understanding of transformation gives the spiritual struggle, particularly in Iranian Sufism, an altogether different character from that of traditional Christian asceticism.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

A comparison with Mahayana Buddhism would be more apt: what is at stake is much less destruction than a raising and transformation of the soul. Through the method and purpose of this spiritual struggle, we may begin to see how the Sufi resolves in experience his deepest confrontation with the ordinary, outward formulation of Islam's fundamental doctrine: tawhid, divine unity. The outcome is a passage from outward to inward tawhid: a metamorphosis of abstract monotheism.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

In its naive or dogmatic form, monotheism sets a Supreme Being, the Ens supremum, above the sum of all beings, rather like adding one more term to the total—x + 1. Instead of a view that merely places absolute Being alongside other beings, there emerges an inward relationship that, at its furthest reach, can be expressed only through paradox, startling excess, or “pious blasphemies” (shath).

The abstract monotheism of outward tawhid finds its resolution in the idea—or, more accurately, the experience—of divine self-revelation, the theophany (tajalli).

This brings us to the whole question of the relationship between the divine Essence, the divine Attributes, and the divine Acts. In fact, it is a relationship of identity: the divine Acts (af'al) are manifestations through which the Attributes appear, and the Attributes themselves are identical with the Essence. Until the seeker reaches this awareness of divine manifestation, he remains caught in duality, in a world of oppositions. That is why the devout monotheist, no less than the dogmatic theologian engaged in argument and debate, is at bottom an unwitting polytheist.

Yet one does not reach this awareness by turning away from the visible and the tangible. One must first recognize them as a veil, then transform that veil into a mirror. The “ordeal of the veil” is overcome when the veil becomes a “mirror of divine revelation” (mir'at-e tajalli).

A new relationship is then established between uncreated Beauty, the archetype, and the beauty that can be seen and felt. Instead of the negative relationship we are accustomed to seeing between Christian asceticism and the Greek sense of beauty, we must speak here of a recognition that gives beauty a prophetic role.

Sufis such as Ruzbihan and Ibn Arabi find a special bond between each prophet and Beauty as a divine Attribute and the supreme form of divine manifestation. Among the most fascinating discoveries is the figure of the Prophet of Islam as Sufism understands him: the prophet of a religion of beauty, whose sayings abound in echoes of Plato.

But theophanies have no limit. The soul finds peace in discovering the secret of divine self-revelation, yet the inexhaustible variety of these revelations keeps it moving, restless with longing. The invitation “Return, O soul at peace” should not be understood primarily as a return that takes place after the soul has become peaceful. The return is the soul's progressive coming to peace. So the certainty of these restless souls grows within their serenity, just as restlessness persists within their peace. They know nothing of the dizzying sense of nothingness or absurdity, or of the panics that drive individuals and crowds into ready-made shelters of dogma, religious or secular.

As Ibn Arabi interprets it, this is not a return to God in general, to a God conceived collectively, but to your own Lord. It marks a radical release of the divine relationship from collective forms, and the emergence of an individual bond between Lord and devoted servant (rabb and marbub), bound up with the sense that spiritual individuality has roots before earthly existence, in eternity itself.
I. Sufism and the Peace of the Soul

The divine Being manifests itself to the believer in a theophany suited to the particular being that believer has possessed within God from before eternity; in revealing that being, God also reveals Himself to Himself. This is the mystery of spiritual individuation (tafrid): at once the passing away (fana') of the nafs ammara, the domineering soul with its possessive instincts, and enduring, intensified existence (baqa') within God's act of revealing Himself to Himself.
